segments.say: Welcome to Code Quest, Chapter 1.
Today you will write and run your first Python program.
segments.subtitle: Write it. Run it.

segments.say: You will also learn to use an AI assistant as a tutor, and to check its work.
segments.subtitle: Write it. Run it. Read the errors. Check the AI.

segments.say: Let's start with a puzzle.
A learner asked an AI assistant to print today's date with hyphens between the numbers.
The AI wrote this single line of code.

ask.question: Will this print `2026-11-09` exactly? Yes or no?

after.say: Here is the real output. There are spaces where the hyphens should be.
The code runs without an error, but it does not do what was asked.
By the end of this video, you will know why, and how to fix it.

segments.say: Here are your five goals for this chapter.
One. Run a Python file and see its output.
Two. Explain how Python runs a program: one line at a time, from top to bottom.
Three. Use print to show text and numbers, and control the spacing.
Four. Read an error message and find the line that caused it.
And five. Ask an AI assistant to explain code in a safe way.

scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Three short ideas, each highlighted while spoken.

visual.heading: Why this matters
items: A **program** is a list of instructions that a computer follows exactly.
Output shows what a program is doing. Developers use `print()` to check their code.
AI can write code.
It is often right, and sometimes wrong while sounding sure.
Researchers who built AI tutors for Harvard's CS50 course saw this too.
**You** run the code. **You** decide if it is correct.

segments.say: Every app you use is a program. A program is a list of instructions that a computer follows exactly.
When a program shows a message, you can see what it is doing. Professional developers often use print to check their code.
AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude can write code.
They are often right. But sometimes they are wrong, and still sound sure.
Researchers who built AI tutors for Harvard's CS50 course saw exactly this.
So who checks the code?

ask.question: An AI wrote your code. Who decides if it is correct?

after.say: You do. You are the person who runs the code, and decides if it is correct.

scenes.title: The idea: Python reads from top to bottom
scenes.direction: Diagram, two key words, the recipe analogy, then a quick check.

visual.heading: How Python runs a program
body: The **interpreter** reads your `.py` file and carries out each line in order.
visual.pre:
You write          Python reads          The computer acts
 +-----------+      +--------------+      +-------------------+
 | hello.py  | ---> |  line 1      | ---> | shows line 1      |
 | (text)    |      |  line 2      |      | shows line 2      |
 +-----------+      +--------------+      +-------------------+
                     top to bottom,
                     one line at a time

segments.say: A Python program is a text file that ends in dot p y. Each line is an instruction.
Python, the program called the interpreter, reads your file.
It carries out each line in order: top to bottom, one line at a time.

visual.heading: Two words you need
items: A **function** is a named action Python already knows. Call it with its name and brackets: `print(...)`.
A **string** is text inside quotation marks: `"Hello"`.

segments.say: Print is a function: a named action that Python already knows. You call it with its name, then brackets.
Text must be inside quotation marks. Text in quotation marks is called a string.

visual.heading: A program is like a recipe
items: The cook follows each step in order, exactly as written.
Where it stops working: a cook can guess what you meant. Python cannot.
A typing mistake makes Python stop and report an error.

segments.say: Think of a program like a recipe. The cook follows each step in order.
But the comparison stops at one point. A cook can guess what you meant. Python cannot.
If a step has a typing mistake, Python stops and reports an error.

visual.question: A file has three `print()` lines. In which order does Python run them?
options: All three at the same time
From top to bottom, one line at a time
visual.explain: Python runs one line at a time, from the first line to the last.

segments.say: Quick check. A file has three print lines. In which order does Python run them? Choose A, B, C or D.

after.say: The answer is B. Python runs your file from top to bottom, one line at a time.

items: A program is a list of instructions.
Python runs them from top to bottom.
Text inside quotation marks is a string.

segments.heading: Step 1: Install Python (3.12 or newer)

segments.say: On Windows, use the Python install manager from python dot org or the Microsoft Store.
On macOS, download the installer package from python dot org and open it.
On Linux, Python is usually installed already.

visual.heading: Check the version in a terminal

segments.say: Then open a terminal and check the version.
On Windows, type python, space, dash dash version.
On macOS and Linux, type python3, space, dash dash version. You should see a line that starts with Python 3.

scenes.title: Steps 2 and 3: Write and run your first file
scenes.direction: The file types itself in line by line as it is explained. The output appears only after the run command.

visual.heading: Step 2: Create your first file
visual.hidden_text: Run it to see the output.

segments.say: Step 2. Open a code editor, such as Visual Studio Code or IDLE, and create a file called ex 0 1 hello.
Line 1 starts with a hash sign, so it is a comment. Python ignores comments. They are notes for people.
Line 2 prints a greeting.
Line 3 prints a second line.
Step 3: run the file. In the terminal, go to the folder that holds your file.
On Windows, type python, then the file name.
On macOS and Linux, type python3, then the file name.
You will see two lines. Each print produces one line of output.
The quotation marks do not appear, because they only mark where the text starts and ends.

scenes.title: Step 4: Check the order
scenes.direction: Type the three steps in, keep them on screen with the question and timer, then reveal.

segments.say: Step 4. This program prints three steps for making tea. Step 1, boil the water.
Step 2, add the tea leaves.
Step 3, pour the tea into a cup.
Before you run it, predict the output.

ask.question: In which order will the three steps appear in the output?

after.say: The lines appear in the same order as the code.
Try this: swap two lines in your file and run it again.
The output changes, because Python always runs from top to bottom.

scenes.title: Step 5: Several values, sep and end
scenes.direction: Settings table with each row in focus, then the code line by line, the question with the code still visible, and the reveal with the matching output line lit.

visual.heading: Step 5: Two settings of `print()`
rows: What goes after the last value

segments.say: Step 5. Print can show several values at once, separated by commas. It also has two settings.
Sep sets what goes between the values. Its default is one space.
End sets what goes after the last value. Its default is a new line.
Look at line 2. The calculation 3 plus 4 has no quotation marks.
Line 3 sets sep to a colon.
Line 4 sets end to three dots, and line 5 prints the word done.

ask.question: What do lines 4 and 5 print together?

after.say: Here is the output. Line 2 has no quotation marks, so Python calculates 3 plus 4 and prints 7.
Line 3 joins the values with colons instead of spaces, so they look like a time.
Line 4 ends with three dots instead of a new line.
So line 5 continues on the same line: Loading, dot dot dot, done.

visual.question: Which setting changes what goes **between** the values in `print()`?
visual.explain: `sep` is the separator between values. `end` is what comes after the last value.

segments.say: Quick check. Which setting changes what goes between the values in print?

after.say: The answer is B, sep. Sep goes between values. End goes after the last value.

items: You can run a Python file from the terminal.
Each `print()` makes one line of output.
`sep` goes between values; `end` goes after them.

scenes.title: Work with AI: a tutor, not a machine
scenes.direction: Safety habits one at a time, then the six stages and two prompt cards. The opening puzzle returns: the question stays beside the code, and the fix replaces the flawed line.

visual.heading: Three safety habits
items: Never paste passwords, keys or private information into an AI tool.
Run every piece of AI code yourself and compare the output with what you asked for.
You are responsible for the code you use, even if an AI wrote it.

segments.say: Use an AI assistant as a tutor that explains, not as a machine that does your work. Follow three safety habits.
One. Never paste passwords, keys or private information into an AI tool.
Two. Run every piece of AI code yourself, and compare the output with what you asked for.
Three. You are responsible for the code you use, even if an AI wrote it.

visual.heading: AI at every stage
columns: How to use AI in this chapter
rows: Ask for the steps of a welcome card in plain English, with no code yet.
Write it yourself first. Then ask AI to explain each line.
Paste the exact output and ask for code that uses only `print()`.
Paste the code and the full error. Ask for the cause before the fix.
Ask AI to compare expected and real output, space by space.
Ask for at most two readability suggestions, each with a reason.

segments.say: AI helps at every stage. Plan the steps in plain English first.
Write the program yourself, then ask for an explanation.
Generate code from an exact output.
Debug with the full error message.
Test by comparing outputs, space by space.
And improve with at most two suggestions.
Try this one.

ask.question: Your program stops with an error. Which stage do you use, and what do you paste?

after.say: Debug. Paste the code and the full error message, and ask for the cause before the fix.

visual.heading: Prompt card: explain, do not rewrite
visual.label: Write
visual.prompt: Here is my Python code: <paste your code>. Do not rewrite it. Explain what each line does in one simple sentence, and tell me if it prints exactly this: <paste the output you want>.
visual.check: Run your program. If the AI said yes but the output differs, trust the real output.

segments.say: Here is the Write card. Paste your code, and ask the AI not to rewrite it.
Ask it to explain each line in one simple sentence, and to say whether it prints exactly the output you want.
Then run your program. If the AI said yes but the output differs, trust the real output.

visual.heading: Prompt card: code for an exact output
visual.label: Generate
visual.prompt: Write Python code that uses only the print() function. It must output exactly these lines, with the same spaces and symbols: <paste the exact output>. Show the code, then show the output it produces.
visual.check: Run the code and compare every character, including spaces, with your target.

segments.say: And here is the Generate card. Ask for code that uses only print.
Paste the exact output you want, with the same spaces and symbols.
Then run it and compare every character, including spaces. This is how the date flaw was caught.

visual.heading: AI pair moment: find the flaw

segments.say: Now, back to the opening puzzle. The request asked for hyphens, but the output has spaces.

ask.question: Which `print()` setting puts a space between the values? How would you change it?

after.say: The AI forgot that sep is a space by default.
The fix sets sep to a hyphen, and now the date prints correctly.
after.heading: The fix: set `sep` to a hyphen

after.say: Always check AI output against what you asked for, character by character.

items: Use AI as a tutor that explains.
Never paste private information.
Run AI code and compare it with your request.

segments.say: Take a breath. You have caught a real AI mistake. That is the most important skill in this course.
Next, the four mistakes that beginners make most often.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: For the first two mistakes, the learner hunts the bug while the code and question stay on screen; then the real error appears.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: spot the problem
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 1. This line should print Good morning. Something is missing.

after.say: The closing quotation mark is missing. Python cannot see where the text ends, so it reports a syntax error.
after.heading: Mistake 1: a missing closing quotation mark

after.say: A syntax error means Python could not read the file, so no line runs.
Add the closing quotation mark before the bracket.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: spot the problem
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 2. Line 2 is fine. Look closely at line 3.

after.say: Print starts with a capital P. Python treats capital P Print and small p print as different names.
after.heading: Mistake 2: a capital letter in `print`

after.say: Notice that Start was printed first. This error happened while the program was running, so the lines before it had already run.
The report names line 3, and the last line even suggests the fix.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: curly quotation marks
visual.note: Curly: `“ ”`   Straight: `" "`   Python accepts only the straight ones.

segments.say: Mistake 3 is curly quotation marks. Word processors and some chat apps change straight quotation marks into curly ones.
Python only accepts straight ones.
Type the quotation marks again in your code editor.
And copy code from a code block, never from a formatted document.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: spot the problem
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 4. One more line that will not run.

after.say: The closing bracket is missing. Every opening bracket needs a closing bracket.
after.heading: Mistake 4: a missing closing bracket

segments.say: Here are all four, side by side. Each one is the last line of its error report.
Unterminated string literal: a quotation mark is missing.
Name is not defined: check the spelling, such as a capital P.
Invalid character: retype the quotation marks.
Was never closed: add the closing bracket.
The habit to build: read the last line first. It names the kind of error. Then look at the line number.

visual.question: An error message has several lines. Which line do you read first?
visual.explain: The last line names the kind of error. Then look for the line number.

segments.say: Quick check. An error message has several lines. Which line do you read first?

after.say: The answer is B, the last line. It names the kind of error.

items: Errors are messages, not failures.
Read the last line first: it names the error.
Then find the line number.

segments.say: One more breather. Errors are normal, and every developer sees them every day.

visual.heading: Recap
items: A program is a list of instructions. Python runs them from top to bottom.
`print()` shows values. Text goes in quotation marks; calculations are worked out first.
`sep` controls what goes between values, and `end` what goes after them.
An error names the kind of error and the line. Read the last line first.
AI is a tutor. Ask it to explain, then run and check everything yourself.

segments.say: Let's recap.
A program is a list of instructions, and Python runs them from top to bottom.
Print shows values. Text goes in quotation marks, and calculations are worked out first.
Sep controls what goes between values, and end controls what goes after them.
An error names the kind of error and the line, so read the last line first.
And AI is a tutor. Ask it to explain, then run and check everything yourself.
